messages.subject_clean: Ordering stacked bar chart
messages.body_plain:
I'm creating a stacked bar plot, but can't get ggplot2 to stack the bars in the order I want, even though I've set the factor levels of the stacking variable to the desired order. The data frame I'm using for plotting is called numCty and is pasted in below using dput. Here's my plotting code:

ggplot(numCty, aes(County, count, fill=Status)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", colour="black", lwd=0.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label=count, y=pos), colour="grey30", size=2.4) +
  coord_flip() +
  xlab("County") + ylab("Number of Projects") +
  labs(fill="Project Status") +
  theme(axis.text=element_text(size=8),
        axis.title=element_text(size=9))

The plot looks exactly how I want it, with one exception: The ordering of the bars is currently (from left to right) green, blue, red (representing Status values of, respectively, Active, Inactive, and Completed). However, the ordering I want is red, green, blue (Status values of, respectively Completed, Active, Inactive).

As you can see in the numCty data frame pasted below, the factor levels of Status are in the order Completed, Active, Inactive, which (I would have thought) should result in ggplot stacking them in that order. Yet, ggplot is ignoring this ordering.

Thanks for any suggestions on how to get the desired ordering of the stacked bars.

Joel

You'll need to sort the data frame first:

numCty <- numCty[order(numCty$County, numCty$Status),]

...after which things plot correctly, except those geom_text labels, which are now out of position. You may want to compute them programatically, something like:

# assumes a sorted data frame
runningsum <- 0
for(i in 2:nrow(numCty)) {
     runningsum <- ifelse(numCty[i,"County"] == numCty[i-1,"County"], runningsum+numCty[i-1,"count"], 0)
     numCty[i,"pos"] <- runningsum + numCty[i,"count"]/2
}
numCty[1,"pos"] <- numCty[1,"count"]/2

Ben

messages.subject: geom_line creates unexplained spikes in a curve
messages.subject_clean: geom_line creates unexplained spikes in a curve
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm making a series of species-accumulation curves which for the most part work as I intend but there is a single line that consistently is producing unexplained spikes around 200 individuals (foodbancs C) - see attached picture. I've tried removing certain parts of the following code, anti-aliasing with Cairo and removing the offending rows (though if you do, you'll see that the line is still perturbed, just differently so)

ES_all  <- read.csv(file="es_comparison.csv", header=TRUE)
#ES_all  <- ES_all[-c(108:112),] ##to remove rows, de-# if needed
region  <- ES_all$Region
active  <- ES_all$site
site  <- ES_all$ID

primcol  <- c("#FF0000","#0066CC", "#006600", "#FFCC33", "#CC00FF")

ESA  <- ggplot(ES_all, aes(x=ind, y=es, group=ID))
ESA  <- ESA + geom_line(aes(colour=(region), lty=(active)), size=1.5)
ESA  <- ESA + theme_bw() + xlab("Individuals") + ylab("Estimated Species Richness") + scale_colour_manual(values=primcol)
ESA  <- ESA + theme(text=element_text(size=17)) + theme(legend.title=element_blank())
ESA  <- ESA + theme(panel.background=element_rect(fill="white"))
ESA  <- ESA + theme(panel.grid.major=element_line(colour="grey"))
ESA  <- ESA + theme(panel.grid.major.x=element_blank())
ESA  <- ESA + theme(panel.grid.minor=element_line(colour="grey")) + theme(legend.position="bottom")
plot(ESA)

Any ideas much appreciated,

Thanks

James

The geom used in the legend is a solid point, so it doesn't have a fill. You can force it to use another symbol, like this:

ggplot(data=df, mapping = aes(x=xx, y=yy)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape=type3, fill=type2), size=5) +
  scale_shape_manual(values=c(24,25,21)) +

  scale_fill_manual( values=c('green', 'red')) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = 21)))

Best,
Ista

z.gnm.plot <- function(modelfit=gnm.emax, se.fit=T, type="response",
                       quan.v=c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.625, 0.75, 0.875, 1)) {

    # data: predicted

     pred.gnm <- predict(modelfit, se.fit=se.fit, type=type)

     pred.df <- data.frame(RESP=pred.gnm$fit, SE=pred.gnm$se.fit, EXPO=model.frame(gnm.emax)[,2],
                           RESP.org=model.frame(gnm.emax)[,1])

     pred.df$CIU <- pred.gnm$fit + 1.96 * pred.gnm$se.fit
     pred.df$CIL <- pred.gnm$fit - 1.96 * pred.gnm$se.fit

     pred.df <- pred.df[order(pred.df$EXPO), ]

     # data: observed

     expo.quan <- quantile(pred.df$EXPO, quan.v, na.rm=T)
     EXPO.grp <- expo.quan[-length(expo.quan)]+diff(expo.quan)/2

     pred.df$EXPOC <- cut(pred.df$EXPO, expo.quan, include.lowest = T)

     TAB.count <- table(pred.df$RESP.org, pred.df$EXPOC)

     PROB <- TAB.count[2, ]/apply(TAB.count, 2, sum)

     obs.ORR.df <- data.frame(EXPOC = EXPO.grp, prob=PROB, logit=log(PROB/(1-PROB)))

     # data: errorbar for observed
        library(binom)

     obs.conf <- binom.confint(TAB.count[2, ], apply(TAB.count, 2, sum), conf.level = 0.95, methods = "prop.test")
     obs.ORR.df$plower <- obs.conf[, 5]
     obs.ORR.df$pupper <- obs.conf[, 6]

     ## plot: prediction line and shade

     gg.pred <- ggplot(pred.df, aes(x=EXPO, y=RESP)) +
       geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=CIL, ymax=CIU), alpha=0.2) +
       geom_line()

     ## plot: prediction line and shade

     gg.obs <- if (type=="response") {geom_point(data=obs.ORR.df, aes(EXPOC, prob)) +
                       geom_errorbar(data=obs.ORR.df, aes(ymin=plower, ymax=pupper), width=.2)
     }

     else {geom_point(data=obs.ORR.df, aes(EXPOC, logit), shape=21, size=3, fill="white")}

     gg.pred.obs <-  gg.pred + gg.obs

     print(gg.pred.obs)
}

Here's a reproducible (hint!) example:

> df <- data.frame(x=rnorm(1000))
> p <- ggplot(df,aes(x))+geom_histogram()
> print(p)
stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth = x' to adjust this.

Note that ggplot warns that it's selected a default bin width. If you want to show frequency, the simplest thing to do is make a density plot:

> p1 <- ggplot(df,aes(x))+geom_density()

If you want a relative histogram, see http://stackoverflow.com/questions/10064080/plot-relative-frequencies-with-dodged-bar-plots-in-ggplot2 and related answers.

In addition to what Doug said, there are two ways to adjust the x axis limits: first, xlim(), which will truncate the data, and second, coord_cartesian(), which 'zooms' in without truncating data.

> # these do not produce the same plot
> p1 + xlim(c(-2,2))
> p1 + coord_cartesian(xlim=c(-2,2))

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

You won't be able to resize panels in facet_grid(). Look carefully at your attached graph, say in column 2; how could you sensibly resize both panels independently and retain some sense of consistency in the display?

There is an example in http://www.nature.com/psp/journal/v2/n10/full/psp201356a.html (see Figure 7) of how to resize facets, but it requires facet_wrap(). You would need to combine your two factors into one (e.g., via paste() or interaction()) so you'd lose the 2D structure of facet_grid(), but then you could resize the panels if you wished.

Personally, I'd leave the present display alone as the missing categories are informative and the structure allows for easy comparison, but the cited article provides an example of how to shrink panels if you want it.

Dennis

messages.subject_clean: Adding a number of lines to a boxplot / sorting (again)
messages.body_plain:
Here is a simplified version on a manufactured (and reproducible) toy data frame:

DF <- data.frame(g = factor(rep(seq(3), each = 50)),
                 y = rnorm(150, mean = rep(c(5, 10, 15), each = 50)))

DF2 <- data.frame(trt = paste0("treat", 1:3),
                  val = c(3, 9, 16))

library(ggplot2)

ggplot() +
   geom_boxplot(data = DF, aes(x = reorder(g, -y, median), y = y)) +
   geom_hline(data = DF2, aes(yintercept = val, color = trt),
                        size = 1, show_guide = TRUE) +
   scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "red", "green")) +
   labs(x = "", color = "treat")

Notes:

1. Since the aesthetics for geom_boxplot() and geom_hline() differ, it is safer to map the aesthetics locally in each geom. Since the data frames differ in each geom, one can also
define the data frames for each plot layer locally.
2. Notice how the reorder() function [in geom_boxplot()] produces descending order by ordering -y rather than y. This is necessary because reorder() does not have a decreasing = argument.
3. By default, geom_hline() does not produce a legend guide. You need to add show_guide = TRUE to the call to get one.
4. It is your responsibility to provide a minimal reproducible example; fortunately, this was a straightforward problem and at least you provided a graph as a template of what you wanted.

Dennis

messages.subject_clean: How to add spike histograms to multiple curves
messages.body_plain:
I have several service functions in the Hmisc package that I'd like to translate to layer functions in ggplot2.  Two of them are scat1d and histSpike.  I have found that spike histograms are better than rug plots for large datasets and want to start with histSpike.  [A spike histogram uses thin lines to indicate relative counts using either unique x values occurring in the data or 100 bins whichever is less and with vertical line lengths proportional to counts, with maximum height of about 0.3 cm.  Spike histograms are effective where there are many curves, even if they intertwine.]  Here is an example goal:
>From data frame A draw two curves (x, y) distinguished by color indicating groups (e.g., female/male).
Compute x values and relative counts for each value of the grouping variable and store them in data frame B (which has 3 variables).
Along each curve drawn in step 1 add the spike histograms using geom_segment() with the vertical segments centered on the curve values (curves are linearly interpolated for this purpose using approx()).  Spikes should be the same color as used for the group variable in step 1.
Any guidance about which attack to use would be appreciated.  I know how to do this when ggplot(aes(...)) does not include the group variable.

As an aside I could not see how to use physical units of measurements with geom_segment for heights of segments.  I guess I need to use something like y range/50 using ggplot_build(ggplot2 object) [I don't know how to sense the y-axis range when the ggplot2 object is not yet complete].

Here is an example:

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-3xJFNd8Gb38/VImYFSL3pMI/AAAAAAAABvM/rQ03uH1TvVY/s1600/z.png>
require(Hmisc)
set.seed(1)
x <- seq(0, 1, by=0.01)
y1 <- x + x^2
y2 <- x - 2*x^3 + 1
plot(x, y1, type='l')
lines(x, y2)
xs <- rnorm(1000, .3, .3)
xs2 <- rnorm(1000, .7, .3)
histSpike(xs, curve=list(x=x, y=y1), add=TRUE)
histSpike(xs2, curve=list(x=x, y=y2), add=TRUE)

Thanks
Frank

Hi Frank:

I took a quick look at histSpike() and it's pretty clear from its return value that you can't pass it directly to ggplot() :)

ggplot2:: stat_bin() is known to be wonky when it comes to computing relative frequencies on a groupwise basis so I wouldn't completely trust it if you want to be able to support counts, proportions and densities. You're better off writing a function to set up the data in a form that is easily passed to ggplot() which you did in your example. I think if you rewrote histSpikes() to return a data frame or list of data frames that you could pass to ggplot() directly, you'd have better luck.

>From what I saw, it looks like histSpikes() determines the axis limits inside the function body. You can take advantage of that to make one data frame for the curves, perhaps another for the x location, top and bottom of the spikes and a third for the limits and return them as a list. The graph could be produced with a function that takes the list as one input argument with others as necessary and then assign them to different data frames inside the function. One of the advantages of ggplot2 is that you can use different data frames to produce different layers and this approach would give you complete control over the contents of the graphic.

To set axis limits, you can use xlim()/ylim() or the limits = argument of scale_(x/y)_continuous(). In the case I'm envisioning, the data frame for the limits would have one line and you could use DF$var to access individual values.

My impression is that you already do the necessary computations in histSpikes() so it's just a matter of organizing the output so that it's easy to pass to ggplot().

Cheers,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dennis,

Thanks for your thoughts.  I've put together a function that seems to be working - code is below preceded by example usage.  I'm addding histSpikeg to the Hmisc package.

f <- lrm(y ~ blood.pressure + sex * (age + rcs(cholesterol,4)),
         data=d)
p <- Predict(f, cholesterol, sex)
g <- ggplot(p, aes(x=cholesterol, y=yhat, color=sex)) + geom_line() +geom_ribbon(data=p, aes(ymin=lower, ymax=upper), alpha=0.2,
                linetype=0, show_guide=FALSE)
g
g + histSpikeg(yhat ~ cholesterol + sex, p, d, ylim=c(-1, 1.25))

histSpikeg <- function(formula=NULL, predictions=NULL, data,
                       xlim=NULL, ylim=NULL,
                       side=1, nint=100, frac=.02) {
  ## Raw data in data, predicted curves are in predictions
  ## If predictions is not given, side (1 or 3) is used
  v  <- all.vars(formula)
  yv <- v[ 1]
  xv <- v[-1]
  if(length(xv) > 2) stop('may not specify more than two predictors')
  if(length(xv) == 2 && ! length(predictions))
    stop('predictions must be given if formula has two variables on the right')
  x1 <- data[[xv[1]]]
  if(length(xlim)) {
    data <- data[x1 >= xlim[1] & x1 <= xlim[2], ]
    x1 <- data[[xv[1]]]
  }
  if(length(unique(x1)) > nint) {
    eps <- diff(range(x1, na.rm=TRUE)) / nint
    x1  <- round(x1 / eps) * eps
  }
  x2 <- if(length(xv) == 2) data[[xv[2]]]
  p  <- predictions
  if(length(p)) xr <- range(p[[xv[1]]], na.rm=TRUE)
  else frac <- frac * 2

  if(length(xv) == 1) {
    tab    <- as.data.frame(table(x1))
    tab$x1 <- as.numeric(as.character(tab$x1))
    tab    <- tab[tab$x1 >= xr[1] & tab$x1 <= xr[2], ]
    tab$rf <- tab$Freq / sum(tab$Freq)
    if(length(p)) tab$yy <- approx(p[[xv]], p[[yv]], xout=tab$x1)$y
  } else {
    tab <- as.data.frame(table(x1, x2))
    tab <- subset(tab, Freq > 0)
    tab$x1 <- as.numeric(as.character(tab$x1))
    tab    <- tab[tab$x1 >= xr[1] & tab$x1 <= xr[2], ]
    tab$rf <- tab$Freq / sum(tab$Freq)
    tab$yy <- rep(NA, nrow(tab))
    for(s in levels(tab$x2)) {
      i <- tab$x2 == s
      j <- p[[xv[2]]] == s
      tab$yy[i] <- approx(p[[xv[1]]][j], p[[yv]][j], xout=tab$x1[i])$y
    }
  }
  tab$rf <- tab$rf * diff(ylim) * frac / max(tab$rf)
  n <- nrow(tab)
  tab$ylo <- if(length(p)) tab$yy - tab$rf
  else if(side == 1) rep(ylim[1], n) else rep(ylim[2], n)

  tab$yhi <- if(length(p)) tab$yy + tab$rf
  else if(side == 1) ylim[1] + tab$rf else ylim[2] - tab$rf
  if(length(xv) == 2) names(tab)[names(tab) == 'x2'] <- xv[2]

  ggplot2::geom_segment(data=tab,
                        aes(x=x1, xend=x1,
                            y=ylo, yend=yhi))
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

When you create a "figure file", it gets saved onto disk, not in the R
workspace. By the same token, you can save an output file onto your
disk. You can always write an R function that saves both the graph and
the data to separate files. For more control over where those objects
get saved, you can include a function argument that specifies the
directory/folder to which they get saved.

If you want to keep the ggplot object and the data file yoked in the R
workspace, have your function return a list object.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
One possible reason for not implementing fill patterns is that they are really not recommended.  They were originally used when the only way to produce high quality graphs was by hand or with a manual pen plotter (where trying to use a solid fill often resulted in holes in the paper).  Tufte in his book discusses that many of the fill patterns can cause a Moire effect when looked at (this is an illusion of movement from still patterns with lots of parallel lines, especially when patterns have different angles).

A probably better approach to moving away from color (many good reasons to do so) is instead to use a dot plot, you can use symbols or more direct labeling rather than worrying about colors or patterns.  Dotplots also work better when you want to include error bars (the bars tend to distort barplots since the focus is on comparing lengths/widths and the added error bar fuzzies up that comparison, with dotplots you are comparing positions on an aligned scale which the bars interfere with much less).

Hi:

Here are three options; there are undoubtedly others.

dat <- data.frame(expand.grid(n=c(50, 100), type=c("A","B"),
                              hor=c(1:24)), ver=rnorm(96))

library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=hor, y=ver)) + geom_point() +

       facet_grid("type ~ n", labeller = label_both) +
       theme(axis.text = element_text(size = rel(1.5)))

# Redefine the breaks
p + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(5, 20, by = 5))

# Artificially expand the limits of the x-range
p + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-2.5, 27.5),
                       breaks = seq(0, 25, by = 5))
# Increase the spacing between panels
p + theme(panel.margin = grid::unit(0.2, "in"))

I prefer the second one, but YMMV.

Hi all,

 I'm having a problem with SVGs exported with ggsave, and wonder whether anyone might have a suggestion. The SVGs use the <def> element, to define common elements, and these common elements are assigned IDs to refer to them. The problem is that while these IDs are unique within each plot, they are not consistent between plots. The result is that if more than one ggsave generated SVG is included in a web-page, then the IDs collide, messing up the plots.

Does anyone know of a way to control the generation of these IDs, say to given them a unique prefix per plot? (Maybe this is not a ggplot2 specific question after all ...)

Thanks in advance for any suggestions,

Jony

Hopefully someone will prove me wrong, but I don't think there are any

sed -i 's/glyph/f1glyph/' test1.svg
sed -i 's/glyph/f2glyph/' test2.svg

depending on your platform, or perhaps

system.time({write(gsub("glyph", "f1glyph", x1),
      file = "test1_fixed.svg")})

if you need to do it within R. Option 3 is beyond my capabilities.

Best,
Ista
